nodes.title: MATERIALIT Y ASSESSMENT
nodes.summary: The text covers materiality assessment, a stakeholder engagement process to identify and prioritize significant issues, enabling resource focus, strategy alignment, risk mitigation, and opportunity leverage. nodes.summary: The Outlook section cites NASSCOM's Strategic Review 2025, projecting 4.3% growth in Indian IT services revenue to US$137.1 billion in FY2025, driven by AI, cloud-native development, and cybersecurity. AI is a key priority, with increased adoption in software development, contact centers, customer experience, knowledge management, and industry use cases. GCC setup, expansion, and transformation in India present significant opportunities. ER&D services are estimated to grow 7% year-on-year in FY2025, driven by innovation, regional manufacturing, and digital engineering with AI/GenAI adoption; in 2024, ER&D had ~47% volume share in large deals led by telecom, automotive, hi-tech, and BFSI, with automobile and digital engineering themes rising ~3x and ~2x year-over-year. Global IT services spending will be driven by vendor consolidation and cost takeout; data and cloud spending remain strong, and core AI spending is expected to increase. Top five digital priorities—AI/ML (including GenAI), cybersecurity, cloud and edge, big data and analytics, and robotics and automation—are anticipated to account for 60%-80% of total digital spend. Increased interest in moving AI and GenAI solutions from proofs of concept to production will accelerate enterprise investments in AI use cases, digital and cloud transformation, and data modernization, creating significant opportunities for IT services. Global IT service providers support enterprises with consulting, business process, and technology services across AI/GenAI, digital transformation, cloud, application development, maintenance and support, data and analytics, cybersecurity, and ER&D. The IT services industry is expected to play a pivotal role in AI/GenAI experimentation and scaled adoption, cost optimization, operational excellence, digital transformation, security advisory and managed services, vendor consolidation, customer experience, product and service innovation, and talent strategies. nodes.title: b) Goodwill

b) Goodwill
The excess of the cost of an acquisition over the Company’s share in the fair value of the acquiree’s identifiable assets and liabilities is recognized as goodwill. If the excess is negative, a bargain purchase gain is recognized in equity as capital reserve. Goodwill is measured at cost less accumulated impairment (if any).
Goodwill associated with disposal of an operation that is part of cash-generating unit is measured based on the relative values of the operation disposed of and the portion of the cash-generating unit retained, unless some other method better reflects the goodwill associated with the operation disposed of.

nodes.title: B) Impairment of Investment in subsidiaries
nodes.summary:
B) Impairment of Investment in subsidiaries
The Company assesses investments in subsidiaries for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the investment may not be recoverable. If any such indication exists, the Company estimates the recoverable amount of the investment in subsidiary. The recoverable amount of such investment is the higher of its fair value less cost of disposal (“FVLCD”) and its value-in-use (“VIU”). The VIU of the investment is calculated using projected future cash flows. If the recoverable amount of the investment is less than its carrying amount, the carrying amount is reduced to its recoverable amount. The reduction is treated as an impairment loss and is recognized in the statement of profit and loss.

For fixed-price development contracts with performance obligations satisfied over time, the percentage-of-completion method is used, based on costs incurred to total estimated costs, with key estimates including future labor costs and productivity. Revenue, profit, and timing are subject to revisions; if progress cannot be reasonably measured, revenue is recognized only to the extent of recoverable costs, and estimated losses are recognized as onerous contract provisions. Contract assets (unbilled amounts dependent on milestones) and contract liabilities (advance consideration) are defined. Maintenance contracts recognize revenue on a straight-line basis for repetitive services or using percentage-of-completion for non-repetitive, discrete services; if invoicing represents value delivered, revenue is recognized based on right to invoice. Fixed-quantum output contracts recognize revenue based on actual output achieved, with residual unutilized service recognized upon completion. Element or volume-based contracts recognize revenues and costs as services are rendered.

a) Current income tax
Current income tax for the current and prior periods are measured at the amount expected to be recovered from or paid to the taxation authorities based on the taxable income for the period. The Company offsets current tax assets and current tax liabilities, where it has a legally enforceable right to set off the recognized amounts and where it intends either to settle on a net basis, or to realise the asset and liability simultaneously.

From time to time, in the normal course of business, the Company transfers accounts receivables, unbilled receivables, net investment in finance lease receivables (financial assets) to banks. Under the terms of the arrangements, the Company either substantially transfers its risks and rewards or surrenders control over the financial assets and transfer is without recourse. Accordingly, on such transfers the financial assets are derecognized and considered as sale of financial assets. Gains and losses on sale of financial assets without recourse are recorded in finance costs, at the time of sale based on the carrying value of the financial assets and fair value of servicing liability. The incremental impact of such transactions on our cash flow and liquidity for the years ended March 31, 2025 and 2024 is not material.

nodes.title: Independent Auditor’s Report
nodes.summary: This Independent Auditor’s Report for Wipro Limited covers the audit of Consolidated Financial Statements, presenting an unmodified opinion that they give a true and fair view under Ind AS. It details the basis for opinion, including compliance with Standards on Auditing and ethics. The key audit matter is revenue from fixed-price contracts using the percentage-of-completion method, addressed through control testing and estimate evaluations. The report outlines management and auditor responsibilities, including risk assessment, going concern, and reporting on legal requirements under Section 143(3), director disqualification, internal financial controls, remuneration, litigations, provisions, investor education fund transfers, fund representations, dividend compliance, audit trail, and CARO. It also includes the auditor’s opinion on internal financial controls over consolidated financial statements, confirming adequacy and effectiveness, with inherent limitations noted. The report concludes with the auditor’s signature and lists sections: Reporting Context, Corporate Overview, Performance and Outlook, Sustainability at Wipro, and Statutory Reports and Financial Statements, which include the Consolidated Balance Sheet as of March 31, 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: OPINION

It presents the Opinion that the financial statements give a true and fair view in conformity with Ind AS. It defines Key Audit Matters and identifies Revenue from fixed-price contracts using the percentage-of-completion method as the key audit matter, referencing specific notes.

nodes.title: Key Audit Matter Description
nodes.summary: The text describes revenue recognition for fixed-price contracts using the percentage-of-completion method, which requires estimating total project costs and involves significant judgment. It explains that estimated losses on uncompleted contracts are provisioned when probable. The matter is identified as a key audit matter due to high inherent uncertainty in estimating efforts to complete, requiring auditor judgment and extensive audit effort to evaluate the reasonableness of estimates supporting revenue recognition.

nodes.title: How the Key Audit Matter was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The text covers the auditor's procedures for key audit matters on fixed-price contracts using percentage-of-completion, including control testing, contract evaluation, and estimate consistency checks. It then addresses other information responsibilities, management and board responsibilities for consolidated financial statements under Ind AS, and the auditor's responsibilities, including risk assessment, internal controls, going concern, and materiality. It also details reporting on legal and regulatory requirements, including compliance with Section 143(3), director disqualification, internal financial controls, director remuneration, pending litigations, provisions, investor education fund transfers, fund representations, dividend compliance, audit trail feature, and CARO reporting with no adverse remarks.

nodes.summary: This auditor's report annexure covers the audit of Wipro Limited's internal financial controls over consolidated financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2025. nodes.title: Wipro Consolidated Financial Statements: Company Overview and Basis of Preparation
key_items: (i) Statement of compliance and basis of preparation
nodes.summary: This page presents the corporate overview and basis of preparation for Wipro's consolidated financial statements. It identifies Wipro as a leading IT services and consulting company, incorporated in India, with listings on BSE, NSE, and NYSE, and notes board authorization on May 22, 2025. The basis of preparation section covers compliance with Ind AS, Schedule III of the Companies Act, and SEBI guidelines, including consistent application of accounting policies and adoption of new standards effective April 1, 2024. It addresses classification of current/non-current assets and liabilities, reporting currency in millions of Indian Rupees, rounding and regrouping notes. The basis of measurement section states use of historical cost and accrual basis, except for derivative financial instruments, certain financial instruments at fair value, defined benefit liability/asset, and contingent consideration and written put options.

nodes.title: (iii) Use of estimates and judgment
nodes.summary: The text details the use of estimates and judgment in preparing Ind AS consolidated financial statements, covering the nature of accounting estimates, their ongoing review, and recognition of changes. It then enumerates specific areas: revenue recognition (including performance obligations, transaction price allocation, percentage-of-completion method, and volume discounts), impairment testing for goodwill and intangibles, income taxes (provision, deferred tax, and realizability), business combinations (identifying intangibles and fair value estimates), defined benefit plans and compensated absences (actuarial assumptions), expected credit losses on financial assets, useful lives of property, plant and equipment, and provisions and contingent liabilities (recognition and disclosure). Finally, it begins material accounting policy information with the basis of consolidation for subsidiaries and controlled trusts under Ind AS 110.

nodes.title: Key Accounting Estimates and Judgments in Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The page covers key accounting judgments and estimates: deferred tax asset realization based on future taxable profits; business combination fair value assessments for intangibles, assets, liabilities, and contingent consideration; defined benefit plans and compensated absences using actuarial assumptions; expected credit losses on financial assets based on default risk and collection timing; useful lives of property, plant and equipment; and provisions and contingent liabilities recognition and disclosure. It also introduces Section 3, Material Accounting Policy Information, specifically the Basis of Consolidation. The text is part of Wipro's consolidated financial statements notes under Ind AS.

nodes.title: Subsidiaries and controlled trusts
nodes.summary: The text covers consolidation principles: control basis per Ind AS 110 for subsidiaries and controlled trusts, including line-by-line consolidation and elimination of intra-group transactions. It addresses non-controlling interests' initial measurement (fair value or proportionate share) and subsequent attribution of comprehensive income. It explains liability recognition for written put options to non-controlling interests. Equity method investments for significant influence (20-50% voting power) are described, including initial cost and share of profits. It also covers functional and presentation currency (Indian Rupees), and foreign currency transactions and translation, including exchange gains/losses recognition, hedging treatment, and non-monetary asset translation.

nodes.title: Consolidation, Non-controlling Interests, Equity Method, and Currency Translation
key_items: Liability for written put options to noncontrolling interests
Investments accounted for using the equity method
nodes.summary: The page covers consolidation principles, including control assessment and elimination of intra-group balances. It details non-controlling interests measurement at fair value or proportionate share, and attribution of comprehensive income. It addresses liability recognition for written put options to non-controlling interests as financial liabilities at present value with equity debit. It explains equity method accounting for investments with significant influence (20-50% voting power), including initial cost recognition and share of profit adjustments. It also covers functional and presentation currency, stating items are measured in functional currency and statements presented in Indian Rupees, and foreign currency transactions and translation.

nodes.title: a) Transactions and balances
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for foreign currency transactions and balances, including translation at transaction and reporting dates, recognition of exchange gains/losses, treatment of borrowings, non-monetary items, and fair value adjustments. It details foreign operations translation, exchange differences in FCTR, disposal treatment, and goodwill adjustments. It also addresses hedging of net investments, intercompany receivables/payables, and ineffective hedge portions. Additionally, it outlines non-derivative financial instruments: definition, initial and subsequent measurement, cash and cash equivalents, and investments at amortised cost.

nodes.title: Foreign Operations, Financial Instruments, and Cash Equivalents
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for foreign operations, including translation of assets, liabilities, income, and expenses into Indian Rupees, recognition of exchange differences in other comprehensive income and foreign currency translation reserve (FCTR), and treatment upon disposal. It also addresses foreign currency differences for hedges of net investments, ineffective hedge portions, and intercompany receivables/payables considered part of net investment. Additionally, it defines non-derivative financial instruments, listing financial assets and liabilities, and their initial and subsequent measurement. Finally, it details cash and cash equivalents, including cash on hand, bank deposits, demand deposits, and bank overdrafts for cash flow and balance sheet purposes.

nodes.title: b. Investments
nodes.summary: The text details accounting policies for investments under Ind AS. It covers debt instruments measured at amortised cost, fair value through other comprehensive income (FVTOCI), and fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL), specifying criteria, income recognition, and disposal treatment. It also addresses equity instruments not held for trading, with irrevocable election for FVTOCI or FVTPL, including fair value movements, disposal gains/losses, dividend recognition, and transfer of cumulative gains/losses to retained earnings upon derecognition. Interest income and dividend recognition are explained for each category.

nodes.title: c. Other financial assets:
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for other financial assets, including their definition, components, presentation, and measurement at fair value and amortized cost. It details trade payables and other liabilities recognition and measurement, including contingent consideration. It also addresses derivative financial instruments, explaining exposure to foreign currency fluctuations, risk management, and recognition at fair value. Three types of hedging are described: cash flow hedges, hedges of net investment in foreign operations, and other derivatives, outlining treatment of effective and ineffective portions, discontinuation, and recognition in other comprehensive income or profit and loss.

nodes.title: Trade Payables, Derivatives, and Hedge Accounting Policies
key_items: d. Trade payables and other liabilities:
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for trade payables and other liabilities, including initial recognition, amortised cost measurement, and contingent consideration. It also details derivative financial instruments, their fair value measurement, and risk management for foreign currency fluctuations. Two hedge accounting types are described: cash flow hedges and hedges of net investment in foreign operations, covering recognition in other comprehensive income, treatment of effective and ineffective portions, and reclassification upon occurrence or discontinuation of the forecasted transaction or hedge.

nodes.title: c. Others
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for foreign currency derivatives not designated as hedges, with fair value changes recognized in profit and loss or finance costs. It details derecognition criteria for financial assets and liabilities under Ind AS 109, including retention of risks and rewards. It then describes equity components: authorized share capital and securities premium, treasury shares held by a controlled trust, retained earnings, capital reserve, capital redemption reserve, share options outstanding account, and Special Economic Zone re-investment reserve, including amounts and restrictions on distribution.

nodes.title: Derecognition of Financial Instruments and Equity Components
key_items: a) Share capital and Securities premium
nodes.summary: The page covers derecognition of financial instruments, including when financial assets and liabilities are removed from the balance sheet and treatment of retained risks. It also details equity and share capital: authorized share capital and securities premium, treasury shares held by a controlled trust, retained earnings, capital reserve, and capital redemption reserve. Each equity component is described with amounts and whether it is freely available for distribution, including comparisons between March 31, 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: f) Share options outstanding account
nodes.summary: The text covers equity-related reserves: share options outstanding (recording equity-settled payments, transferred to securities premium upon exercise) and Special Economic Zone re-investment reserve (created from eligible SEZ unit profits under Section 10AA for plant and machinery acquisition, not freely distributable). It details foreign currency translation reserve (exchange differences from foreign operations, long-term inter-company balances, hedging instruments, and foreign currency borrowings recognized in OCI net of taxes), cash flow hedging reserve (effective hedge fair value changes in OCI), and others (fair value changes of financial instruments at FVOCI and actuarial gains/losses on defined benefit plans in OCI). Dividend policies (final dividend liability on shareholder approval, interim on board declaration) and buyback of equity shares (recorded as reduction of securities premium and retained earnings, with capital redemption reserve created) are explained. Bonus issue treatment (transfer from reserves to share capital) is noted. Property, plant and equipment recognition (measured at cost less depreciation/impairment, capitalizing borrowing costs, derecognition on sale), capital work-in-progress, and depreciation methods (straight-line over useful life, leasehold improvements over shorter of life or lease term, term licenses over contract term, freehold land not depreciated) are covered.

nodes.title: Notes on Reserves, Dividends, Buyback, Bonus, and PP&E
nodes.summary: The page covers reserves including foreign currency translation (exchange differences, hedging, net investment hedges), cash flow hedging (effective derivative changes), and others (FVOCI financial instruments, actuarial gains/losses). It details dividend recognition (final as liability on shareholder approval, interim on board declaration), buyback of equity shares (reduction of securities premium and retained earnings, capital redemption reserve creation), and bonus issue (transfer from reserves to share capital). It also includes property, plant and equipment recognition, measurement, de-recognition, cost capitalization of borrowing costs, derecognition on disposal, and capital work-in-progress measurement.

nodes.title: b) Depreciation
nodes.summary: The text covers depreciation policies for property, plant and equipment, including straight-line depreciation over estimated useful lives, amortization of leasehold improvements and term licenses, and non-depreciation of freehold land. It lists useful lives for asset categories (buildings, plant and equipment, computer equipment, furniture, vehicles), reviews lives annually, and justifies deviations from Schedule II. It addresses component accounting, capitalization of subsequent expenditure, and classification of capital advances and work-in-progress. It also details business combinations using the purchase method, including acquisition cost, contingent consideration, and transaction costs. Goodwill measurement, impairment, and allocation on disposal are explained, along with intangible assets' initial measurement, amortization, and useful life review.

nodes.title: Accounting for PP&E, Business Combinations, and Goodwill
key_items: (vii) Business combinations, Goodwill and Intangible assets
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for property, plant and equipment (PP&E), business combinations, and goodwill. It details estimated useful lives for various asset categories, review and adjustment of useful lives, component accounting, capitalization of subsequent expenditure, and classification of capital advances and work-in-progress. For business combinations, it describes the purchase method, measurement of acquisition cost, recognition of identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, expensing of transaction costs, and treatment of contingent consideration. For goodwill, it explains recognition as the excess of cost over fair value of net assets, bargain purchase gains, impairment measurement, and allocation upon disposal of operations within cash-generating units.

nodes.title: c) Intangible assets
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting for intangible assets, including measurement at cost for separately acquired assets and fair value for those from business combinations, followed by cost less amortization and impairment. It explains that amortization reflects expected economic benefits, useful lives are reviewed annually, and lists useful lives: 1–10 years for customer-related intangibles (customer contracts and relationships from business combinations) and 2.5–10 years for marketing-related intangibles (vendor relationships and brand from business combinations).

nodes.summary: (viii) Leases

nodes.title: The Company as a lessee
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for leases, inventories, and impairment. As a lessee, it details lease identification, term assessment, recognition of right-of-use assets and lease liabilities, measurement, depreciation, impairment, and remeasurement. It also addresses short-term and low-value lease exemptions. As a lessor, it covers finance versus operating lease classification and intermediate lessor accounting. Inventories are valued at lower of cost (weighted average) and net realizable value. Impairment policies include expected credit loss model for financial assets with lifetime or 12-month allowances, and non-financial asset impairment testing for long-lived assets and goodwill, including recoverable amount determination and loss recognition.

nodes.title: Lease Accounting, Inventories, and Impairment Policies
nodes.summary: The page covers lease accounting from the lessor's perspective, including classification as finance or operating leases and treatment of intermediate lessors with separate head-lease and sub-lease contracts. It addresses inventory valuation at lower of cost (weighted average) and net realizable value, with provisions for obsolescence. It also details impairment for financial assets using the expected credit loss model, covering amortized cost assets, FVTOCI debt instruments, trade receivables, unbilled receivables, finance lease receivables, and other financial assets. It explains measurement of loss allowances: lifetime expected credit loss for trade, unbilled, and finance lease receivables using a provision matrix with risk profiling and forward-looking adjustments, and twelve-month expected credit loss for other financial assets unless credit risk significantly increased.

nodes.title: b) Non-financial assets
nodes.summary: The text covers non-financial asset impairment and employee benefits. It details impairment assessment for long-lived assets (PP&E, RoU, intangibles) when indicators exist, and annual goodwill testing at cash-generating unit level. Recoverable amount is higher of fair value less cost of disposal (using turnover/earnings multiples) and value-in-use (projected cash flows). Impairments are recognized in profit or loss, and reversals are allowed for long-lived assets but not goodwill. Employee benefits include post-employment plans classified as defined contribution or defined benefit. Defined benefit obligations use projected unit credit method, with remeasurements in OCI and net interest in profit or loss. Specific plans described: provident fund (defined benefit trust and defined contribution government fund) and gratuity/foreign pension (defined benefit, partially funded, third-party managed).

nodes.title: Employee Benefits: Post-Employment Plans and Provident Fund
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for employee benefits, focusing on post-employment plans classified as defined contribution or defined benefit. It explains recognition of expenses, actuarial valuation using projected unit credit method, remeasurements in other comprehensive income, and net interest calculation. It also details the provident fund plan, where employer and employee contributions are made to a company-managed trust (accounted as defined benefit due to liability for shortfall) or government-administered fund (accounted as defined contribution). The text includes a note on impairment reversal for assets other than goodwill.

nodes.title: B. Gratuity and foreign pension
nodes.summary: The text covers employee benefits: gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, with a third-party managed fund; foreign pension plans per country regulations, partially funded and third-party managed, providing monthly or lump-sum payouts, with obligations actuarially valued using the projected unit credit method; superannuation as a defined contribution scheme with annual contributions; termination benefits expensed when no longer withdrawable; short-term benefits like bonuses and profit-sharing measured on an undiscounted basis and expensed as service is provided, with liabilities recognized for probable obligations; compensated absences allowing carryforward or cash at retirement, with accumulating absences actuarially valued and non-accumulating recognized when incurred; share-based payments including equity and cash-settled instruments, measured at fair value, expensed over vesting with accelerated amortization, and cash-settled re-measured; and provisions recognized for present obligations from past events with probable outflows and reliable estimates.

nodes.title: Employee Benefits and Share-Based Payment Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for employee benefits and share-based payments. It details defined benefit plans using actuarial valuation, defined contribution superannuation, termination benefits expensed when no longer withdrawable, short-term benefits like bonuses and incentives measured on an undiscounted basis, and compensated absences including accumulating and non-accumulating types with actuarial valuation. It also covers share-based payment transactions, including equity and cash-settled instruments, measured at fair value at grant date, expensed over vesting periods, with cash-settled instruments re-measured at each reporting date.

nodes.title: (xiii) Provisions
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for provisions and revenue. Provisions are recognized for present obligations from past events where outflows are probable and estimable, measured at best estimate considering risks. Reimbursements are recognized as assets when virtually certain. Onerous contracts provisions are measured at present value of lower of net cost of fulfillment or termination cost. Revenue primarily comes from software development, maintenance, consulting, business process services, and IT product sales. Revenue is recognized upon transfer of control using a five-step approach: identify contract, identify performance obligations, determine transaction price, allocate price, and recognize revenue. Collectability uncertainty postpones recognition. Performance obligations are assessed for distinctness and allocated based on stand-alone selling prices or residual method. Over-time revenue is recognized using progress measures, with methods varying by contract type: time and materials (as services rendered) and fixed-price development contracts (percentage-of-completion based on costs incurred).

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition and Contract Types in Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The page covers provisions for onerous contracts and third-party reimbursements, then details revenue recognition under Ind AS. It defines revenue sources (software development, maintenance, consulting, BPS, IT products) and the five-step model: identify contract, performance obligations, transaction price, allocate price, and recognize revenue upon satisfaction. It addresses collectability uncertainty, assessing distinct performance obligations, and allocating transaction price using stand-alone selling prices or residual methods. For over-time obligations, revenue is recognized by progress measures. It categorizes contracts into time and materials (revenue recognized as services rendered) and fixed-price contracts.

nodes.title: i. Fixed-price development contracts
nodes.summary: The text details revenue recognition policies: fixed-price development contracts use percentage-of-completion based on cost inputs, with contract assets/liabilities and loss provisions; maintenance contracts recognize revenue straight-line, percentage-of-completion, or right-to-invoice, including fixed quantum contracts; element/volume-based contracts recognize revenue as services are rendered; product sales recognize revenue upon transfer of control; and contract modifications are accounted for based on distinctness and pricing, either cumulatively or prospectively.

nodes.title: Earnings per share
nodes.summary:
Earnings per share
Basic earnings per share is computed using the weighted average number of equity shares outstanding during the period adjusted for treasury shares held. Diluted earnings per share is computed using the weighted average number of equity and dilutive equivalent shares outstanding during the period, using the treasury stock method for options, except where the results would be anti-dilutive.
The number of equity shares and potentially dilutive equity shares are adjusted retrospectively for all periods presented for any splits and bonus shares issues including for change effected prior to the approval of the consolidated financial statements by the Board of Directors.

nodes.title: Wipro Financial Risk Management: Market Risk and Procedures

The company's exposure arises from investment, borrowing, and foreign currency revenue activities, with the goal of avoiding excessive earnings and equity losses. Risk management procedures are handled by a corporate treasury department, which independently controls market risk management, recommends objectives and policies approved by senior management and the Audit, Risk and Compliance Committee, manages cash resources, implements hedging and borrowing strategies, and ensures compliance with risk limits and policies.

nodes.title: a) Transactions and balances
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting for foreign currency transactions and balances. Transactions are translated at the exchange rate on the transaction date. Net losses on borrowings are in finance expense; net gains in finance and other income. Non-monetary items at historical cost are translated at the transaction date rate. Translation differences on non-monetary financial assets at fair value, such as equities through OCI, are included in other comprehensive income, net of taxes.

nodes.title: b) Foreign operations
nodes.summary:
b) Foreign operations
For the purpose of presenting consolidated financial statements, the assets and liabilities of the Company’s foreign operations that have a functional currency other than Indian Rupees are translated into Indian Rupees using exchange rates prevailing at the reporting date. Income and expense items are translated at the average exchange rates for the period. Exchange differences arising, if any, are recognized in other comprehensive income and held in foreign currency translation reserve ("FCTR"), a component of equity, except to the extent that the translation difference is allocated to non- controlling interest. When a foreign operation is disposed of, the relevant amount recognized in FCTR is transferred to the consolidated statement of income as part of the profit or loss on disposal. Goodwill and fair value adjustments arising on the acquisition of a foreign operation are treated as assets and liabilities of the foreign operation and translated at the exchange rate prevailing at the reporting date.

nodes.title: a) Financial assets
nodes.summary: The Company uses the expected credit loss model to recognize impairment losses on financial assets measured at amortized cost, debt instruments classified as FVTOCI, trade receivables, unbilled receivables, finance lease receivables, and other financial assets. Expected credit loss is defined as the difference between contractual and expected cash flows, discounted at the effective interest rate. For trade, unbilled, and finance lease receivables, loss allowances are measured at lifetime expected credit loss using a provision matrix based on customer risk profiles and historical loss experience adjusted for forward-looking information. Other financial assets use twelve-month expected credit loss unless credit risk significantly increased, then lifetime expected credit loss applies.

c) Short-term benefits
Short-term employee benefit obligations such as cash bonus, management incentive plans or profit-sharing plans are measured on an undiscounted basis and are recorded as expense as the related service is provided. nodes.title: Sale of financial assets
nodes.summary:
Sale of financial assets
From time to time, in the normal course of business, the Company transfers accounts receivables, unbilled receivables and net investment in finance lease receivables (financial assets) to banks. Under the terms of the arrangements, the Company either substantially transfer its risks and rewards or surrenders control over the financial assets and transfer is without recourse. Accordingly, on such transfers the financial assets are derecognized and considered as sale of financial assets. Gains and losses on sale of financial assets without recourse are recorded in finance expenses, at the time of sale based on the carrying value of the financial assets and fair value of servicing liability. The incremental impact of such transactions on our cash flow and liquidity for the years ended March 31, 2023, 2024 and 2025 is not material.
